title: Recruitment software for staffing agencies by features and fit
summary: Discover the best types of recruitment software for staffing agencies. Explore must-have features, how to compare platforms, and how to avoid common selection mistakes.
body_markdown:
Recruitment software gives agencies a centralized platform for finding and screening candidates, tracking them through the pipeline, and managing client and candidate communication.


Crucially, agency software offers important features that a corporate in-house tool doesn’t. Agency platforms expand on the capabilities of standard ATSs or recruiting CRMs with the tools agencies need, like multi-client workflows, back-office operations, and permission controls that wall off one candidate’s data from another.


Compare those needs to those of an in-house shop, where there’s one employer and a clear-cut pipeline end point, and you quickly understand why agencies need dedicated software. Here’s how to choose.


## **Must-have features for agencies**


Agency software manages recruiting and back-office functions within one integrated system. Consider separating the two functions, as software that excels in one area usually lacks in the other.


### **Recruiting and relationship management**


Features that aid recruitment and help manage client relationships:


- **Applicant tracking:** Recruitment orders, resume parsing, and tracking for each submission.
- **Recruiting CRM:** Client relationship management and the various interactions of job, candidate, and client.
- **Job order management:** Track status for open reqs and fulfillment across clients.
- **Candidate ownership rules:** Candidate relations management, specifically around ownership.
- **Outreach tracking:** Integrated tracking for all outreach (email, calls, etc.) across teams.


### **Operations, automation, and controls**


Agency software includes operations-specific features that differentiate it from more general[recruitment software](https://juicebox.ai/blog/recruiting-software-comparison) :


- **Scheduling and time tracking:** Shift assignment, mobile clock-in, and timecard approval for contingent placements.
- **Payroll, invoicing, and contracts:** Rules for payment and billing, and automated invoice generation based on the hours you scoped.
- **Onboarding and compliance:** Generate and track federal and state employment compliance forms.
- **Integrations:** An open API and staffing-specific integrations for background checks, job boards, and VMS systems.
- **AI assistance:**[Automation](https://juicebox.ai/blog/recruiting-automation-tools) of routine tasks, like outreach and call transcriptions.
- **Client portals and security:** Branded client access points with permissions to protect each client’s data.


## **How to compare staffing platforms**


Ask yourself these kinds of questions before requesting a single demo:


- How many recruiters do you have on staff? How many are permanent hires vs contract?
- What’s your placement volume?
- What steps in the recruiting process do you lose the most time to?


The answers bear directly on the type of[recruiting tool](https://juicebox.ai/blog/recruiting-tools-for-hiring-teams) that’s best for you.


### **Compare core platform fit**


Remember, demos are an opportunity for vendors to showcase their buzziest features. Don’t over-index on them. An effective buyer consideration set starts with your actual workflows, constraints, and needs, working backwards from there to evaluate tools against a consistent set of criteria.


Things to check when assessing platform fit:


- Applicant tracking and CRM depth
- Sourcing
- Outreach
- Client portal
- Back-office depth


### **Compare practical trade-offs**


Feature set is just one side of the coin. A few practical considerations to ask about before signing a vendor MSA, in rough order of importance:


- Onboarding/implementation length
- The migration process
- Reporting depth, including whether you need a separate analytics tool
- Integrations with your existing stack
- Seat minimums, automatic renewals, and other contract or pricing risks


## **Pricing and cost considerations**


There’s enough variation in the way recruitment agency software vendors price their products to warrant understanding what it looks like at a high level before making a decision.


A few basic models:


- **Per-user pricing:** Costs scale with the number of seats needed.
- **Flat-rate pricing:** Costs are pegged to your specific product tier without consideration for the number of individual seats.
- **Quote-based pricing:** Extremely common at the enterprise level; also seen with platforms offering back-office modules.
- **Free access, with product restrictions:** Free-to-paid models that give you the basics but require a commitment to unlock advanced features or capabilities.


Be aware that, when it comes to pricing at least, what you see isn’t always what you get. Some platforms charge annually without a monthly option. Others enforce minimum-seat requirements that can have you paying for capabilities you don’t need yet. Always check for one-time add-ons, like implementation charges, and job limits that cap the number of reqs you can post at once.


## **Common software agency mistakes**


The following are the common mistakes for agencies to keep in mind during the procurement process.


### **Selection and fit mistakes**


Agencies often fail in choosing the right tool when they expect one platform to cover multiple use cases, like sourcing, screening, and pipeline tracking, equally well.


For starters, choosing a generic or mismatched tool can lead to failing one of the basic requirements identified earlier: the ability to track both candidate and client workflows in one tool. Other agencies default to corporate ATS platforms that work well when you have a sizable employer brand and attracting inbound volume isn’t a problem, but fail entirely to account for[outbound sourcing](https://juicebox.ai/blog/best-sourcing-tools-for-recruiters) when that’s not the case. Right-size selection criteria to the realities of your agency first.


### **Implementation and adoption mistakes**


Messy data is a non-starter for implementation, and “cleaning up” your database by migrating the mess won’t truly solve the problem. Make sure to audit and dedupe before exporting.


Ensure the active recruiting team is pulled into the process early, too. Exclusion leads to recruiters working out of spreadsheets and deprives the larger org of the data it needs to justify the new tool.


Early over-customization locks in faulty workflows before users learn the limits of the platform. Finally, get clear on what you want/need AI features to do before evaluating specific options. Otherwise, highly polished demos can distract selection committees from the core parameters they identified earlier.


## **Software recommendations by staffing model**


Staffing model, not feature set, helps answer the platform question for you. There’s no universal “best-fit” tool, because the answer depends on the type of placements you do.


Recruiters working in different industries likely grasp this intuitively, but it bears repeating. At the end of the day, there’s little overlap in requirements for a healthcare staffing agency running thousands of locum tenens fulfillments across the country, and those of a boutique agency covering a handful of executive placements for enterprise SaaS clients.


That said, there are two broader categories whose needs are similar enough to help guide platform selection at a high level.


### **High-volume and temp staffing platforms**


Agencies in this category need platforms that are strongest in features like shift scheduling, time tracking, payroll, onboarding, and compliance.


Volume is a determining factor here. Agencies that place hundreds of workers every week deal with significant constraints, like short-notice call-offs and heavy turnover, and the math only works when process requirements aren’t a bottleneck, either. Placements need quick onboarding, pay configuration, and to be billed at the right markup. Errors can compound quickly, so platforms need features that over-index on accuracy and speed. An agency that serves a distribution center prepping for the peak season is a classic example.


Compliance needs stack up similarly; take the example of a healthcare staffing agency that has to contend with licensing and credentialing that are strict enough to block an assignment the day they go stale.


### **Direct-hire and specialized search platforms**


Agencies in this category need platforms that are strongest in CRM depth, relationship tracking, client development, and outbound sourcing.


The reason is scarcity. Low-volume and long cycles mean searches that rest on a shortlist of a dozen people and client relationships that take years to develop. The platform’s main job under such constraints is holding history rather than pushing volume. Retained[executive search](https://juicebox.ai/blog/best-candidate-sourcing-tools-for-executive-search) is a clear example, where a candidate who declined two years ago is probably the best call today.


For these agencies, the most-pressing gap to address is sourcing. Specialized firms work with small, mostly employed candidate pools that aren’t actively applying anywhere. ATS and CRM platforms are built to manage candidates you've added to your database, which leaves the top of the funnel to a dedicated sourcing layer.

## **FAQs**


### **What is the best software for staffing agencies?**


There’s no universal best platform, because the right fit depends on your staffing model.


High-volume and temp agencies are best served by platforms that integrate the front and back office, and where scheduling, time tracking, and pay live in the same place recruiting does. Direct-hire and search firms need CRM depth and client development tools, usually paired with a dedicated sourcing platform.


### **How much does recruitment software for agencies cost?**


Cost varies depending on the type of pricing model favored by the platform. Popular pricing models include per-month, flat-rate, and custom quotes, or free-to-paid, with the best features or expanded scope locked behind a payment. All-in prices are often subject to factors like seat minimums, annual billing, or other contract terms, so request a quote covering everything, including implementation costs.


### **Should an agency use an all-in-one platform or several tools?**


All-in-one platforms reduce integration overhead and keep data in one place. But most agencies usually end up adopting one core platform, plus one or two specialist tools. One reason why: agencies that depend on outbound sourcing often find centralized platforms struggle to fill top-of-funnel needs, and choose to supplement the core tool with a sourcing platform to help close the gap.
